nuisance

/NOO-sens/ — rhymes with goose + sense · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A nuisance is a person or thing that causes minor trouble or irritation.

The dripping faucet was a small nuisance that kept everyone awake.

Example

Every morning at 7 a.m., construction workers outside the school made a terrible racket right during first period; classes weren't canceled, but the noise was a constant nuisance that made it difficult for everyone to concentrate.

Nuisance captures the mild-to-moderate annoyance perfectly here — the construction isn't a disaster or a health hazard, just an ongoing source of trouble and inconvenience. A word like 'problem' would be too strong; 'annoyance' is close but lacks the sense of ongoing inconvenience.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

annoyance: An annoyance is anything that mildly but repeatedly irritates — the word points at the feeling it stirs in you. A nuisance is the thing itself: the ongoing source of minor trouble and inconvenience, the dripping faucet, the yapping dog. An annoyance describes your reaction; a nuisance keeps interfering with your day.

inconvenience: An inconvenience causes minor extra trouble — a detour, a form to fill out twice — and the word is neutral about feelings. A nuisance adds the emotional edge: trouble that keeps irritating you while it inconveniences you. An inconvenience costs a little time; a nuisance costs time and patience.

impediment: An impediment is something that blocks or slows progress toward a goal — the word measures obstruction, not irritation. A nuisance is smaller and more emotional: it annoys and inconveniences without truly stopping anything. An impediment stands in your way; a nuisance merely irritates you along the way.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

blessing: something that brings welcome good fortune

convenience: something that makes life noticeably easier

Where it sits · how much trouble it causes

oversight → nuisance → hindrance → catastrophe

oversight vs. nuisance: An oversight is weaker than a nuisance: an oversight is a small mistake nobody intended, while a nuisance actively keeps annoying and inconveniencing people.

hindrance vs. nuisance: A hindrance is stronger than a nuisance; a nuisance merely annoys you, while a hindrance genuinely blocks or slows your progress.

catastrophe vs. nuisance: A catastrophe is vastly stronger than a nuisance: a nuisance is a dripping faucet, while a catastrophe is the whole dam breaking.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — nuis (nocere): to harm, to hurt (Latin, via Old French nuire/nuisance)

Suffix — -ance: state, act, or thing that does (French, from Latin -antia)

Put it together: Nuisance is built on nocere, 'to harm': around 1400 a nuisance meant a real injury or harm. Over the centuries the word softened, so today a nuisance merely annoys and inconveniences rather than truly hurts.

Use the root in a new word: innocent: The jury deliberated for two full days before finding her innocent on every charge.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Nuisance describes something annoying and inconvenient, but definitely not serious — it's the dripping faucet, not the flooded basement. Use inconvenience for practical difficulty or disruption; use nuisance when there's emotional annoyance attached to ongoing trouble.
